
--- PAGE 1 ---
Master’s Thesis
Wearable IMU sensor-based motion
tracking for post-stroke motor impairment
assessment during activities of daily living
Author:
Tanguy Lewko
Supervisor(s):
Dr. Prabhat Pathak, Ph.D.
James Arnold, Ph.D. Candidate
Advisor(s):
Prof. Conor Walsh, Ph.D.
Prof. Auke Ijspeert, Ph.D.
Harvard Biodesign Lab

Private and Confidential - Harvard University - Not for public disclosure

--- PAGE 2 ---
Abstract
Post-stroke individuals face challenges incorporating their affected arm into activities of daily living
(ADLs) due to impairments in motor function. Although task-oriented occupational therapy is a proven
solution for enhancing functional skills, stroke survivors often struggle with motivation and lack feed-
back when attempting to increase the use of their affected arm during everyday activities. Continuous
monitoring of ADLs is a viable solution to provide feedback on the quantity and quality of impaired arm
functional movements and to promote adherence to home rehabilitation programs. Recent advances
in machine learning and wearable inertial measurement units (IMUs) offer promising opportunities for
remote monitoring of rehabilitation training. While the prior art has focused primarily on quantifying
the usage of the affected arm, a comprehensive assessment of rehabilitation progress requires evaluating
movement quality during functional tasks. The objective of this research is thus to develop a wear-
able IMU sensor platform to segment and evaluate stroke survivors’ upper extremity motions during
ADLs.
We leveraged two open-source IMU datasets to develop initial algorithms for assessing movement qual-
ity during ADLs. The first dataset contained healthy participants performing six unimanual upper
extremity self-care ADLs and was used to develop a deep learning algorithm for precise time segmen-
tation of ADLs. We developed a hybrid architecture combining convolutional and bidirectional long
short-term memory layers to extract spatial and temporal information from the input IMU data. Our
algorithm employs dense labeling for time-step resolution segmentation at a frequency of 33 hertz, while
integrating past and future knowledge into current predictions through a context-aware framework. We
achieved F1 scores of 0.83 and 0.87 in across-subjects and within-subjects evaluations, respectively. Ad-
ditionally, we determined that segmentation accuracy was highest when using only the accelerometer
and gyroscope data from two IMU sensors attached to the forearms. We also proposed a methodology
for collecting an annotated naturalistic IMU-based ADL dataset in a controlled environment, using
video ground truth to reliably label ADLs. To demonstrate the feasibility of our activity segmentation
algorithm, we collected a dataset of 5 healthy participants and 5 post-stroke participants. We tested our
algorithm on two mildly impaired post-stroke participants, highlighting the potential need for tailored
models for post-stroke individuals due to the high variability of impairments within the population. The
second open-source dataset was used to extract samples of healthy and post-stroke participants wearing
IMUs on their upper body while drinking and brushing their teeth. We identified robust kinematic
metrics that can be computed directly from accelerometer and gyroscope data and that differentiate
between healthy and stroke participants. Finally, we developed a novel data-driven movement quality
rating scale, the motion healthiness score (MHS), to incorporate identified metrics into a framework
for naturalistic motion quality assessment. The MHS utilizes the Mahalanobis distance to measure
the disparity between the movement of a stroke survivor and the same movement executed by healthy
subjects. It showed desirable properties such as high consistency when rating sample motions from
the same subject and good separability (>80% accuracy) between healthy and post-stroke individuals.
The MHS offers an opportunity to assess impairment in a functional setting without evaluation by a
therapist.

--- PAGE 8 ---
Chapter 1
Introduction
Stroke is a significant cause of long-term disability worldwide. According to the World Health Orga-
nization (WHO), 15 million people worldwide suffer from a stroke every year, with 5 million resulting
in death and another 5 million causing permanent disability, placing a burden on individuals, families,
and the healthcare system. Over 143 million years of healthy life are lost each year due to stroke-related
death and disability. The lifetime risk of stroke has increased over the last 20 years by 50% and is now
one in four people [1]. There are two main types of stroke: ischemic and hemorrhagic. Ischemic strokes
are caused by an obstruction of blood flow to the brain. Due to the lack of blood flow, the brain cannot
get enough oxygen and nutrients, and brain cells begin to die within minutes. Hemorrhagic strokes are
caused by sudden bleeding in the brain. Leaked blood puts pressure on brain cells, damaging them.
Both types can lead to neurological impairments that affect motor function, sensation, and cognition.
Stroke survivors often suffer from physical disabilities like paralysis or weakness on one side of the body,
reduced fine motor skills, and limited range of motion due to muscle stiffness [2]. After six months from
a stroke, about 65% of patients are unable to use their affected hand for their usual activities [3].
Stroke rehabilitation aims to increase patients’ functional independence at home and in the commu-
nity [4]. The central nervous system has some plasticity and can re-organize its connections to recover
degraded cognitive and motor functions. These changes can be favored by learning and practice [5].
Post-stroke progressive, skilled motor practice is critical for continued skill gains, as shown by neu-
roimaging studies [6, 7]. Task-oriented occupational therapy is thus a reliable and safe way to improve
functional skills and quality of life in patients [8, 9]. Occupational therapists (OTs) work to facilitate
and improve motor control in people who have had a stroke by making them practice activities of daily
living (ADLs). These tasks include self-care tasks such as showering, dressing, toileting, and laundry
as well as self-feeding tasks such as meal preparation, eating, and drinking.
From a functional perspective, there are three main consequences of stroke in the upper extremity
(UE) [10]: learned nonuse, learned bad use, and forgetting. Initially, nonuse results from stroke-related
impairments, but as time goes by, it can become a learned behavior. Learned nonuse refers to the
acquired behavior of avoiding the use of the paretic arm during ADLs, even if it could be used, due to the
development of a habit of not using it at all. Learned bad use describes the reinforcement of an abnormal
motion strategy because it helps to perform tasks despite impairments. Finally, forgetting explains the
fact that strokes can lead to transient retention of new skills despite extensive practice, causing even
small practice breaks to lead to terrible rehabilitation results. A good functional rehabilitation program
should aim to train the patient regularly while ensuring that they do not learn abnormal motion.
Although traditional home exercise programs developed by therapists can improve compliance, they
often lack long-term monitoring and feedback, reducing motivation over time [11]. Recent advances
in machine learning and wearable inertial measurement units (IMUs) provide opportunities for remote
monitoring of home-based rehabilitation training, which can be a viable solution to provide feedback on
impaired arm functional movement quantity and quality and foster adherence to home rehabilitation
1

--- PAGE 9 ---
Master’s Thesis
programs. While prior work on wearable sensor-enabled interventions has focused mainly on quantifying
the use of the affected arm [12, 13], a comprehensive assessment of rehabilitation progress requires
evaluating movement quality during functional tasks. The objective of this research is thus to develop
a wearable IMU sensor platform to segment and evaluate stroke survivors’ upper extremity motions
during daily activities. We decompose this objective into three research questions (RQ).
RQ1 How can we reliably segment in time a subset of upper extremity ADLs using IMU sensor
data?
RQ2 Can we identify robust IMU-based kinematic metrics that differentiate between healthy and
stroke participants during upper-extremity ADLs?
RQ3 How can we incorporate identified metrics into a framework for naturalistic motion quality
assessment?
In Chapter 2, we review the prior art that uses wearable IMU sensors to monitor arm movements
after stroke. Then, in Chapter 3, we explain how we developed an upper-extremity ADL segmentation
algorithm that utilizes IMU sensor data, using an open-source dataset of ten healthy subjects performing
ADLs. Chapter 4 presents our protocol and methods for collecting a dataset of healthy and post-stroke
participants performing ADLs. The participants perform naturalistic activities of daily living in a
controlled environment. In Chapter 5, we demonstrate the proof-of-concept of our activity segmentation
algorithm in two mildly impaired post-stroke participants. In Chapter 6, we leverage a second open-
source dataset to determine a set of robust task-specific metrics that differentiate healthy and post-
stroke motions during three component movements within common ADLs: brushing teeth, drinking
transport, and drinking recovery. In Chapter 7, we establish a framework for computing the quality of
motion of stroke patients during various activities of daily living. This framework calculates the motion
healthiness score and measures the Mahalanobis distance to healthy motions.

--- PAGE 10 ---
Chapter 2
Prior art on wearable sensors for
post-stroke upper extremity
rehabilitation at home
Individuals post-stroke often experience motor impairments, and kinematic assessment is an objective
method of quantifying and understanding these impairments. It helps occupational therapists estab-
lish customized rehabilitation programs, monitor progress, and develop new solutions due to a better
understanding of post-stroke motion deficits. Healthcare professionals use standardized impairment
measures to evaluate patients’ functional ability and determine the most appropriate treatment plan.
These include the Functional Independence Measure (FIM), the Modified Barthel Index (MBI), the
Upper-Extremity Fugl-Meyer Assessment (UEFMA), the action research arm test (ARAT), the Wolf
Motor Function Test (WMFT), and others. Among these, the UEFMA is one of the most commonly
used assessments. It evaluates various aspects of motor function, including range of motion, coordi-
nation, and strength. Motion capture systems can provide precise kinematic assessments. In contrast
to visual evaluation by a therapist, they enable objective numeric evaluations of movements and can
complement traditional kinematic assessments.
Optoelectronic motion capture systems are widely regarded as the most accurate and reliable method
for capturing human movement data. They use multiple cameras to localize reflective markers placed
on the body, providing accurate 3D motion data for joints. These systems are reliable in very controlled
environments, but they are high-cost and necessitate large space requirements and extended training and
setup, so they cannot be used easily outside of the lab. Inertial measurement units (IMUs) are wearable
sensors that combine measurements from accelerometers, gyroscopes, and sometimes magnetometers,
allowing the measurement of accelerations, angular velocities, and sensor orientation. While kinematic
joint angles and/or positions can be estimated from sensor fusion of the sensors within an IMU, there
are complications such as drift that make IMUs less accurate than optical motion capture systems. A
great advantage of IMUs compared to motion capture systems is that they are easy to set up and use
outside the lab. All data are collected on the device and can be synced after hours of wearing the
IMUs.
Kim et al. (2021) conducted a review on the use of wearable sensors for assessing and treating upper-
extremity after stroke [14]. They emphasize that wearable sensors can broaden the scope of assessing
UE movements beyond clinical settings. This could enable assessments to be carried out in home set-
tings. Wearable sensors have created numerous possibilities for continuously obtaining measurements
related to rehabilitation, rather than just at specific intervals with in-clinic assessments. Wang et
al.[15] conducted a systematic review of wearable-sensing devices designed for upper-body rehabilita-
tion. Accelerometers and IMUs were the predominant sensing technologies used, comprising 84% of the
3

--- PAGE 11 ---
Master’s Thesis
articles reviewed. Common attachment points were the trunk, upper arm, forearm, wrist, and fingers.
Despite the proliferation of wearable systems, the paper also highlights the scarcity of clinical evalua-
tions performed. This points to the importance of more thorough research to provide evidence on the
effectiveness of these technologies in real-world clinical settings.
Immediately following a stroke, patients tend not to use their affected upper limb in daily living, which
can lead to learned non-use [10]. Initial nonuse occurs because of hemiparesis or sensory loss. When
nonuse becomes habitual, even for activities the affected arm can do, nonuse can become a learned
behavior. This phenomenon is detrimental to rehabilitation because it limits progress and could lead
to forgetting already relearned abilities. Tracking and providing feedback on arm use quantity with
wearable sensors can help reduce learned nonuse and has been the focus of numerous works. Most
studies differentiate between functional and non-functional use of the arm. Functional use includes
goal-directed motion, while non-functional use includes balancing the arms while walking or conver-
sational gestures. David et al. (2021) [13] used two wrist-worn IMUs to compute a gross movement
score to quantify arm use. They were able to detect functional activities with 50-60% accuracy and
eliminate non-function activities with 90% accuracy. They showed that the arm use of the five stroke
patients was biased towards the nonimpaired arm and that stroke participants had reduced total arm
use compared to healthy controls. Bailey et al. (2014) used wrist-worn accelerometers to assess bilateral
UE activity during ADLs and used two variables, the bilateral magnitude and the magnitude ratio, to
distinguish between unilateral and bilateral UE tasks [16]. The general arm use computed from the
accelerometer was found to have good psychometric properties and high correlation with FMA scores
[17, 18, 19]. Zambrana et al. (2019) proposed a hierarchical approach using inertial sensors to first
distinguish between arm movement and non-movements using a threshold-based algorithm and then
between functional movements and non-functional movements using machine learning, in five ADLs and
walking [20]. They achieved accuracies of 0.91 and 0.9 in intra and inter-subject testing. Lum et al.
(2020) also showed the superiority of machine learning models compared to standard threshold-based
algorithms because they are better at distinguishing functional and non-functional arm use [21].
In addition to using wearable sensors to assess paretic arm use, other studies have also explored the
effects of newly developed algorithms coupled with regular feedback on arm usage given to stroke
survivors wearing wearable sensors. The acceptability of such systems has also been investigated in
a small population of post-stroke individuals. Rubio Ballester et al. (2015) [12] developed a low-cost
wearable bracelet to motivate stroke participants to use the paretic arm more by providing feedback
on the activity of the paretic arm. Giving feedback led to increased paretic arm activity, and post-test
activity without feedback was higher than pre-test activity. Their study confirmed that monitoring
the amount of arm use may increase the value of using the paretic limb and that repetitive exposure
to reinforcement-based feedback may modify an individual’s goal and self-representation. Chae et al.
(2020)developed a home rehabilitation system to record the type and frequency of exercises performed
by the user using a smartwatch and ML algorithms [22]. They found that their system was able
to facilitate participation in in-home training and improved the functional scores measured with the
Wolf Motor Function Test and the Upper Extremity Fugl-Meyer Assessment in 17 post-stroke subjects.
Da Silva et al. (2018) conducted a study to analyze the activity responses of seven stroke patients
who had recently suffered a stroke, within 28 days [23]. Patients were given a vibrating alert from a
triaxial accelerometer wristband to prompt movement of the impaired arm if their hourly activity level
decreased. The therapists and patients reviewed the movement activity data twice a week to determine
a personalized prompt threshold. The mean activity increase following a prompt ranged from 11% to
29%. The authors also conducted a pilot randomized controlled trial [24]. In another study by Whitford
et al. (2020), feedback only affected the perceived quantity of arm use and not actual arm use in eight
post-stroke participants [25]. Although this is a less positive outcome, the authors state that perception
of arm use can serve as a necessary first step in building awareness of paretic limb use and promoting
the necessary behavioral changes to reduce nonuse. Lee et al. (2018) [26] developed an approach to
detect both goal-directed movements during ADL and to determine appropriate feedback during two
structured in-home rehabilitation exercises using two wearable sensors. They tested their algorithm
on 20 stroke participants and proposed a feedback method to promote high-dose motor practice by
4 Tanguy Lewko , 7.3.2024

--- PAGE 12 ---
Master’s Thesis
providing a reminder to try to use the affected arm at the time of a movement performed with the
unaffected arm and based on relative arm usage throughout the day. In a survey, 91.7% of occupational
therapists expressed willingness to use the system in their practice. Furthermore, 88.2% of stroke
survivors indicated that they would use the system if recommended by their therapist. These results
demonstrate the demand for such systems.
Parnandi et al. (2021) have developed a detailed way to quantify post-stroke UE rehabilitation training
[27]. They use a deep learning algorithm, taking as input data IMU sensor data and counting the
primitives of motion. Primitives of motion are the building blocks of functional upper extremity motions
that have been developed by Schambra et al. (2019) [28]. Five primitives of motion were identified:
reach, reposition, transport, stabilize, and idle.
Most of the literature on wearable IMU sensors used for home UE rehabilitation of post-stroke survivors
focuses on measuring the extent to which the paretic arm is being used throughout the day, thereby
focusing on nonuse. However, little research has been done on analyzing movement quality during
ADLs, which is essential for a comprehensive assessment of rehabilitation training, also targeting bad
use. This is a challenging task given the important role of contextual information on the activity being
performed for giving a person relevant feedback [13]. In Chapter 3, we develop an algorithm to segment
UE ADLs from IMU sensor data to enable such analysis.
5 Tanguy Lewko , 7.3.2024

--- PAGE 13 ---
Chapter 3
IMU-based segmentation of
upper-extremity ADLs
During therapy, occupational therapists watch patients accomplish ADLs and assess their performance
compared to what the motions would look like like if they were to be done by a healthy person, using
this analysis to suggest exercises targeting weaknesses. The knowledge of the task being done is essential
for feedback and identifying abnormal behaviors. In this chapter, we develop an algorithm to segment
UE ADLs using wearable IMU sensors in healthy participants.
Segmenting activities can offer numerous advantages to a motion monitoring system, encouraging stroke
patients to train their paretic arm. First, it allows for targeted immediate feedback for recognized
activities that can replace generic suggestions. For example, once we identify that patients are using
their unaffected arm for an activity, we could encourage them to use their paretic arm. Moreover,
it facilitates the computation of contextual, task-specific metrics, providing insights from qualitative
and quantitative data. Once we know what activity is being performed, we can compute metrics and
compare them against normative healthy data to characterize motor impairments. Detecting activities
can enable consistent tracking of repeated activities throughout the days, offering valuable progression
metrics for rehabilitation.
Activity recognition through wearable sensors for the upper body remains an underexplored paradigm.
The complexity arises from the high variability in upper body motions, where individuals may perform
the same activities differently. Most lower-body activities such as standing, sitting, walking, or running
repetitive and cyclical which enables clear definitions, but upper-body activities are harder to define.
For example, people often reach from different initial positions to different final positions which affects
how many different "reach" motions look. The beginning and end of a reaching motion can be difficult
to identify as people may move their arms continuously. Additionally, data labeling for upper body
motions is much more expensive as UE ADLs tend to be short. Finally, non-functional motions such
as conversational and non-task-oriented gestures have a significant variance, making it more likely to
misclassify motions.
We start by giving an overview of datasets and algorithms for IMU-based segmentation of upper-
extremity ADLs in Section3.1.
3.1 Dataset and literature review
3.1.1 Datasets in upper body ADL segmentation
There is a shortage of datasets whose data could be used to train models for recognizing upper body
activities of daily living. The challenge arises from the need for standardized activity definitions, with
6

--- PAGE 14 ---
Master’s Thesis
the same activities often described in multiple ways, and from the variability of selected activities.
Additionally, labeling data has a high cost since people perform many different short-duration motions
consecutively. The number of IMU sensors, placement, sampling rate, and other parameters also vary
greatly between datasets.
Boukhenoufa et al. (2022) provided an overview of the latest advances in the use of wearable devices to
collect data and machine learning algorithms to evaluate exercises [29]. This article provides valuable
information on the main challenges faced by researchers in this field. The primary challenge is the
limited quantity and quality of data, as the number of patients available for study is often restricted,
and data collection can be a burden for them.
Finding open-source datasets well-suited for activity segmentation, especially tailored for stroke pa-
tients, poses an even more significant challenge. This is why, despite the ultimate goal being activity
segmentation for stroke patients, the initial focus is on datasets involving healthy individuals. Addi-
tionally, there is a need to identify and categorize activities from the non-paretic arm of stroke patients,
making it also worth detecting motions from an arm without impairment.
We now review existing open-source datasets for upper body activity segmentation and highlight their
strengths and weaknesses.
Multi-Sensory Dataset [30]
Ruzzon et Al. (2020) introduced a multi-sensory dataset related to activities of daily living [30]. The
dataset acquisition involved ten healthy volunteers, right-handed and aged between 22 and 28, who
performed 180 ADL instances while wearing six 9-axis IMUs (two for each arm, one on the back, and
one on the right thigh). The activities were labeled from videos recorded by an RGB camera, and the
labels include both the activity name and the arm performing the featured uni-manual activities.
The featured activities are gathered in Table 3.1, as well as the event defining the start and the end of
the activity:
Task Start End
Walk First leg movement Both legs stop
Sit Down Adjust vertical position to sit Sitting posture is relaxed
Stand Up Shift body weight from chair to feet Standing at normal height
Open Door Hand touches the handle Door is fully open
Close Door Hand contact Door is closed
Pour Water Touching the bottle Hand releases the bottle
Drink Glass Hand contact on the glass No contact with the glass
Brush Teeth Toothbrush touches the teeth Toothbrush leaves the mouth
Clean Table Hand-table contact Contact with the table ceases
Table 3.1: Activities featured in the Multi-Sensory dataset
Due to its detailed activity labels and the variety of activities being performed, this dataset holds
excellent value for activity recognition. However, this dataset has weaknesses. It features a limited
demographic representation with only ten young adult right-handed participants. This might limit the
generalizability of the dataset to a broader population as the execution of daily activities may vary
across age groups and handedness. It does not feature bi-manual tasks. The data is collected in a
controlled environment, i.e., all participants perform activities in the same room setting, which might
limit home-based activity representation.
StrokeRehab Dataset [31]
The StrokeRehab dataset [31] features 22 males and 28 females who have undergone stroke. 22 are
right-side paretic, and 28 are left-side paretic. The age distribution of the patients has a mean of 58.4
7 Tanguy Lewko , 7.3.2024

--- PAGE 15 ---
Master’s Thesis
(SD=13.0), and the mean time since the participants had a stroke is 5.4 years (SD=6.1). Participants
took the Fugl-Meyer upper extremity assessment with a mean score of 42.8 (SD = 15.8). Six of them
have a severe impairment level (FMA 0-25), 25 moderate (FMA 26-52), and 19 mild (FMA 53-65) [32].
The participants performed five times the following set of ADLs: brushing teeth, putting on deodorant,
combing hair, drinking, and vertical and horizontal transports. Each ADL is performed with all its
preparatory actions. For example, the drinking ADL consists of opening the bottle, pouring water into
a glass, taking a sip, and closing the bottle. Twenty controls also performed the same tasks as the
stroke participants. All participants wore a set of nine IMUs attached to the cervical vertebra C7,
the thoracic vertebra T12, the pelvis, and both arms, forearms, and hands. The data also includes
processed joint angles estimated from the IMUs. While this dataset is extremely valuable as it features
stroke participants, its usability is diminished because of the absence of video or motion capture ground
truth. Except for some very salient motions, isolating motions within an activity is challenging, which
prevents us from using this dataset for activity recognition but makes it suitable for some qualitative
analysis of stroke patient motion.
OPPORTUNITY Dataset [33]
The OPPORTUNITY dataset was devised to benchmark human activity recognition algorithms. Data
is collected from daily living activities using a combination of body-worn sensors, object sensors, and
ambient sensors in a smart-home environment.
Four participants perform 16 activities: opening and closing doors, the fridge, drawers, and the dish-
washer, cleaning the table, drinking from a cup, and toggling a switch. While this dataset is used to
benchmark many activity recognition algorithms, the featured actions make it less interesting than the
Multi-Sensory Dataset as the greater part of the actions are similar, and the number of subjects is
smaller.
PAMAP2 [34]
The PAMAP2 Physical Activity Monitoring dataset contains data on 18 activities performed by nine
subjects wearing three inertial measurement units: one on the wrist of the dominant arm, one on the
chest, and one on the dominant side’s ankle. This dataset is also often used to benchmark activity
recognition algorithms from IMU sensors. However, it mainly features lower extremity activities like
walking, running, and cycling, and only a few manual activities (e.g., ironing, vacuum cleaning, and
folding laundry). It has only one sensor for detecting arm motions.
Conclusion on datasets for upper body ADL segmentation.
Datasets suited for upper-extremity ADL segmentation from wearable sensors are not common and all
substantially different, featuring different activities and sensor placements. Our review of the available
datasets revealed that the most interesting dataset we can use to develop our algorithm is the Multi-
Sensory Dataset, as it comprises a pertinent set of self-grooming and self-feeding activities performed
with both hands, with 5 IMU sensors on the upper body (two per arm and one on the back) and
adequate labeling of the ADLs being performed.
3.1.2 Algorithmic approaches for wearable IMU activity segmentation
Evaluating state-of-the-art approaches to upper body activity segmentation from wearable sensors
presents a challenge due to the absence of a reference benchmark dataset encompassing a diverse range
of upper extremity activities. Across various works, datasets vary in the number of sensors employed
and their placement on different body parts. Furthermore, these studies assess different activities, and
even when activities overlap between two datasets, their definitions may differ. For example, an ac-
tivity labeled as eating could involve using a spoon, chopsticks, or hands. Additionally, some papers
include a null category that contains every other activity that is not among the activities of interest.
8 Tanguy Lewko , 7.3.2024

--- PAGE 16 ---
Master’s Thesis
In contrast, others focus on differentiating within classes of interest, leading to much higher reported
accuracy.
This review goes beyond focusing solely on upper body activities, encompassing more work utilizing
wearable IMU sensors for activity recognition. We separate this review into two categories of algorithms:
deep learning algorithms and other algorithms, which typically rely on various machine learning algo-
rithms and pattern recognition algorithms.
Non deep-learning algorithms
The following discusses non-deep learning approaches to recognizing human activities using wearable
sensors, including methods such as pattern recognition and machine learning algorithms.
Lemmens et al. (2015) [35] used multi-array signal feature extraction and pattern recognition algorithms
with 2D convolution to recognize upper extremity activities such as drinking, eating, and brushing hair
from the 3D accelerometers, gyroscopes, and magnetometers attached on the dominant hand, wrist,
upper arm, and chest of 30 healthy participants and one stroke patient. Their algorithms showed perfect
accuracy for the stroke patient under standardized conditions. Still, they were much less effective under
daily life conditions due to the high variation in how actions were performed, showing the limitations
of such pattern recognition algorithms. Huynh et al. (2007) [36] investigated the use of different
machine learning models, namely K-means, nearest neighbor, support vectors machine (SVM), and
hidden Markov models (HMM), to detect both three high-level activities (preparing for work, going
shopping, doing housework) and 16 low-level activities that are part of the high-level activities (e.g.
drive car, eat, iron, brush teeth) from three accelerometers placed on the right wrist, the righthand side
of the hip and the right thigh. They tested the different algorithms on a 10-hour naturalistic dataset,
with slightly better accuracy than 80% for low-level activities and 92% for high-level activities.
Bao and Intille (2004) [37] collected user-annotated data from 20 subjects wearing five biaxial accelerom-
eters. Several classifiers were tried using handcrafted features, such as mean energy, frequency-domain
entropy, and correlation of acceleration data. The mean recognition accuracy was greater than 80% in
20 daily activities (both related to the upper body and the lower body). A study by Chen et al. (2021)
[38] tested different machine learning algorithms (Decision Tree, SVM, XGBoost) to detect 19 different
upper extremity ADLs. XGBoost gave the best results, giving a 90% accuracy on the seven ’easiest’
tasks to detect and with no null class. Yang et al.(2008) [39] proposed a distributed recognition method
to classify actions using a low-bandwidth wearable motion sensor network. Their main contribution
was showing that the distribution of multiple action classes satisfies a mixture subspace model, with
one subspace for each. Reyes-Ortiz (2013) [40] collected a dataset of static and dynamic lower-body
ADLs carried with a waist-mounted smartphone with embedded inertial sensors. They used multiclass
SVM, showing an accuracy of 96% over six lower-body ADLs.
Deep-learning algorithms
Although the first deep learning algorithm was first developed in the 1960s by Ivakhnenko and Lapa[41],
the field has gained popularity only in the last decade, due to the increase of available computational
resources through the development of Graphics Processing Units (GPUs) and Tensor Processing Units
(TPUs), coupled with the development of techniques to train deep neural networks more effectively, like
backpropagation [42]. Since the breakthrough made by AlexNet [43], deep learning has been proven
effective in various fields, including computer vision, natural language processing, speech recognition,
and time series forecasting. Of particular interest to us is its application in human activity recogni-
tion.
Achieving high performance in deep learning is a challenging and iterative process. It involves consider-
ing many combinations of parameters, while an exhaustive grid search across parameters is impractical
due to limited computer resources. The design choices range from data input methodologies, such as
window length, stride, context inclusion, and preprocessing, to broader architectural decisions involving
9 Tanguy Lewko , 7.3.2024

--- PAGE 17 ---
Master’s Thesis
layer types, count, and width, as well as choices related to optimizers, learning rates, and the incorpo-
ration of data augmentation. These parameters are usually chosen by integrating knowledge specific
to the field in the design choices and doing empirical validations on the dataset. The initial step to-
wards developing accurate models is to synthesize existing knowledge. We therefore review the different
methods used to segment upper body activities from wearable sensor data.
Various architectural choices are commonly used for Human Activity Recognition using wearable sen-
sors. Among these, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are frequently employed. CNNs have
demonstrated exceptional performance in various applications, including image classification, speech
recognition, and natural language processing [44]. Recurrent neural networks have also shown encour-
aging results in various domains. These networks are specifically designed to consider the temporal
dependencies of the data. They are commonly utilized in tasks like analyzing time series data for
speech recognition and natural language processing. Hybrid models that leverage both CNN and RNN
layers to integrate the strengths of each type have also demonstrated significant potential.
Hammerla et al. (2016) [45] extensively reviewed deep, convolutional, and recurrent models across
three wearable sensor datasets. They point out that while convolutional neural networks work well
with long and repetitive activities such as walking or running, recurrent neural networks should be
favored for short-duration activities with a natural ordering as they benefit from contextualizing ob-
servation across long periods. Yin et al. (2022) [46] developed a 1-D convolutional neural network
(CNN)-based bidirectional long-short-term memory (bi-LSTM) parallel model with attention mecha-
nism, which outperformed CNN and RNN models in classification accuracy and computational time
complexity on UCI (lower body activities: standing, sitting, laying, walking, downstairs, upstairs) and
WISDM HAR (lower body activities: walking, upstairs, downstairs, sitting, standing, jogging) datasets.
Baloch et al. (2022), introduced two sensor fusion strategies, early and late sensor fusion utilizing a
CNN and a CNN-LSTM [47]. Their findings indicate that a late sensor fusion model based on CNN-
LSTM enhances the recognition accuracy in similar activities. Panwar et al. (2019) [48] used a CNN
architecture to classify three upper limb movements of the human arm, extension, flexion, and fore-
arm rotation, to measure rehabilitation progress. The input data was the triaxial acceleration of the
wrist. Their approach outperformed the classical ML algorithm on this task. In a recent study, Gomez-
Arrunategui et al. (2022) used a single wrist-worn IMU to identify reaching movements in two datasets:
a functional assessment dataset that involved functional assessment tasks, and an Activities-of-Daily-
Living (ADL) dataset that included tasks like pizza-making and walking [49]. The study involved 12
stroke patients, and the researchers used a CNN to classify the different activities. The trained clas-
sifiers performed better when trained and evaluated using standardized functional assessment tasks.
Additionally, the researchers noted that algorithms developed using data collected in clinical settings
may not be as effective when applied to data collected in home environments. Kyritsis et al. (2020)
[50] used a convolutional recurrent neural network to detect bites and used the bites distributions to
determine the start and end of meals. David et al. (2023) [51] used an LSTM-RNN neural network
to recognize six upper-extremity activities in stroke-affected participants by computing 20 handcrafted
features. Kaku et al. (2022) [52] implemented a sequence-to-sequence model to predict the sequence of
motion primitives from wearable sensor data. Zhu et al. (2018) [53] research aimed to detect high-level
ADLs using temporal semantics and used a Sequence-to-Sequence model, too. High-level ADLs are
complex activities consisting of temporal-dependent gestures, such as making coffee. Abdel-Salam et
al. (2021) [54] reviewed top-performing techniques in human activity recognition based on wearable
sensors. They concluded that hybrid approaches relying on both CNN and LSTM layers lead to the
best performance.
Self-supervised learning has also shown promising results in Human Activity recognition due to its re-
duced dependence on labeled data. Zhang et al. (2023) reviewed the different self-supervised learning
frameworks for time series analysis: generative-based, contrastive-based, and adversarial-based frame-
works [55]. Taghanaki et al. (2021) [56] trained a neural network on raw accelerometer data to predict
the value in the z-dimension using past value of this dimension as well as past and present motion
in x and y dimensions. They then froze the model and transferred it to a supervised human activ-
ity recognition network. Their algorithm outperformed state-of-the-art in multiple datasets. Overall,
10 Tanguy Lewko , 7.3.2024

--- PAGE 18 ---
Master’s Thesis
self-supervised learning is worth investigating when we have access to a large quantity of unlabeled
data.
While most existing work focuses on classifying a pre-segmented window as part of an activity, little
work has investigated the precise time segmentation of continuous, non-pre-segmented data. In the first
case, the algorithm is expected to give a label to a whole window that contains only one activity; in
the latter, the window might have multiple activities, and the algorithm is expected to determine the
starting and ending points of the activities precisely.
This task has been studied slightly more in video data, in which it is referred to as Temporal Action
Segmentation (TAS) [57].
3.2 Data preparation
To begin with, we synchronized the Multi-Sensory dataset by combining the data from each IMU sensor
and aligning it with the labels. We have identified six UE ADLs that we want to segment as classes.
These include Open Door, Close Door, Pour Water, Drink Glass, Brush Teeth, and Clean Table. Any
other motion, such as Standing Up, Sitting Down, or Walking, is considered part of the negative class
and we do not train the algorithm to detect those activities. Our algorithm uses the raw acceleration
and gyroscope data as input, which was recorded at an IMU sampling frequency of 33 Hz.
Time series windowing for activity segmentation
The initial step in the activity recognition process is to segment the input signal. Human Activity
Recognition (HAR) algorithms generally take a set of fixed-length segments, known as windows of
signal, as input, and then associate one or more predicted labels with each window. These algorithms
process each window separately in a sliding window framework. In this context, we explain the different
informed choices that we make for our time series windowing framework.
The conventional method for labeling time series data for machine learning models and neural networks
typically involves assigning a single label to each window. This approach is called sliding window
labeling. The label is often determined by either the majority of timesteps within the window (see
Figure 3.1), or the label of the last timestep. While adequate for specific tasks, such as continuous
activities like walking or running, or scenarios where only the occurrence of a particular event matters,
this approach proves less suitable for tasks involving the segmentation of fine motions. In such cases,
the compromise on time resolution becomes a limitation.
To overcome this limitation, we have adopted a dense labeling framework [58]. In this framework, each
time step is assigned a label, which the neural network must predict accurately. This approach enables
precise segmentation at the timestep level. As shown in Figure 3.1, the comparison between sliding
window labeling and dense labeling highlights the benefits of the latter. However, the cost of using
dense labeling is an increase in complexity. The neural network is required to make many inferences to
handle the finer granularity of the data.
11 Tanguy Lewko , 7.3.2024

--- PAGE 19 ---
Master’s Thesis
Figure 3.1: Sliding window labeling vs. dense labeling. Dense labeling is better for fine action segmen-
tation due to its ability to contain multiple labels in each window, allowing for more granularity.
Two critical parameters frequently discussed are window length and stride, illustrated in Figure 3.2.
Window length should ideally encompass a sufficient duration of motions to capture essential contextual
information. For tasks involving fine-grained motions, it is desirable for the window to cover entire
actions unless dealing with rhythmic actions like brushing teeth or cleaning a table, where its repetitive
structure allows for information extraction without the necessity of the entire activity duration.
Figure 3.2: Windowing a time-series: window length, stride and overlap. Window length defines the
size of each window, stride determines the step size between consecutive windows, and overlap specifies
the amount of shared data points between adjacent windows.
Banos et al. (2014) [59] showed that large window sizes do not necessarily translate into better recogni-
tion performance and that optimal window length is activity-dependent. Jaén-Vargas et al. (2022) [60]
showed that for the detection of walking, sitting to standing and squatting, small windows (0.20-0.25s)
showed similar performance as bigger ones (1-2s) while the inference time could be reduced by a factor
4 for LSTM and 2 for the CNN-LSTM model from windows of 100 frames (1s) to 20 frames (0.2s).
While this result does not translate to upper-body activities, which include more semantics, especially
for precise segmentation, it still points to the critical trade-off between window length and processing
time. For upper-extremity activities, researchers tend to use longer windows of a few seconds to capture
UE ADL patterns.
Established knowledge assumes that introducing overlap between consecutive windows helps prevent in-
formation loss at boundaries during training. However, Dehghani et al. (2019) [61] compared the use of
non-overlapping windows and overlapping windows and showed that the performance improvements us-
ing overlapping windows reported in literature seem to be associated with the subject-dependent nature
of the cross-validation process used. For subject-independent training, they concluded that when using
subject-independent cross-validation, no improvement was found using overlapping windows.
12 Tanguy Lewko , 7.3.2024

--- PAGE 20 ---
Master’s Thesis
We introduce a windowing framework designed for context-aware predictions. The objective is to avoid
making predictions at window boundaries, where contextual information tends to be lacking. Leveraging
both the left and right boundaries, representing past and future inputs, we enhance the model’s capacity
to predict labels at the center of the window, improving the predictive capabilities through a more
comprehensive contextual understanding. Figure 3.3 illustrates the context-aware framework.
Figure 3.3: Context-aware prediction framework.
We use windows of 180 timesteps, corresponding to 5.45s, as it allows our algorithm to capture the
temporal dependencies of upper extremity actions. We use the first 60 timesteps (1.82s) and the last 60
timesteps as context, and only the 60 middle timesteps are each paired with a corresponding label.
Managing imbalanced datasets
In multi-label classification scenarios, datasets often exhibit a substantial imbalance in the representa-
tion of each class label, i.e., specific labels occur much more frequently than others. Exposure to such
imbalanced datasets can lead to model bias. Instead of discerning the distinctive features in the data
that characterize the majority class, the model may somewhat default to predicting the majority class.
This tendency arises because, in some cases, solely predicting the majority class and disregarding all
other classes can yield better accuracy than trying to distinguish between all classes.
Standard solutions to the data imbalance challenge include random oversampling, undersampling, and
weighted loss functions. Random undersampling removes instances from the majority classes until a
more balanced distribution is achieved. This method was proven particularly effective in HAR with a
large null class [44]. However, in some cases, particularly with smaller datasets, this method may result
in a less accurate representation of the majority classes due to the potential loss of important informa-
tion. On the contrary, random oversampling involves duplicating examples from minority classes. This
strategy proves advantageous, especially for small datasets, as it avoids information loss. Nonetheless,
a potential drawback is the risk of overfitting, given that exact replicas of examples are created. This
could cause the model to memorize the examples instead of developing generalizable boundaries. Lastly,
weighted loss functions can increase penalties for misclassification in the minority class. The weights can
be inversely proportional to the frequency of classes. Doing so encourages the model to prioritize and
improve its performance in underrepresented classes, fostering a more equitable learning process.
We opt for random oversampling due to the relatively small size of our dataset. We randomly sample
the data with replacement until each class is represented by a minimum number of samples equal to the
number of samples present in the majority class divided by 1.5, allowing us to balance all the classes
we want to segment.
13 Tanguy Lewko , 7.3.2024

--- PAGE 21 ---
Master’s Thesis
Figure 3.4: Classes distribution before oversampling.
Figure 3.5: Classes distribution after oversam-
pling.
3.3 Architectures and model selection
Obtaining an excellent performance in deep learning is an iterative and complex process. Indeed, there
are a lot of parameters to take into account. There is a trade-off, as we cannot do an exhaustive grid
search of parameters due to the computational resources in each model training, but we still want to
reach the highest accuracy possible. We need to select the features to use as input to the model, the
type of architectures and the natures of the layers being used, the number of layers and their width, the
optimizer, learning rate, choice of data augmentation, etc. Often, we try to include as much knowledge
from the field as possible to avoid trying many underperforming pipelines. We try to justify each choice
either from literature or from experiments.
3.3.1 Validation strategies
Validation strategies are essential when assessing a model’s performance, particularly in the context
of upper body activity detection. The distinctive nature of datasets for such activities lies in the
variability of how individuals perform the same activities. Subjects may exhibit variations in motion
speed, employ different combinations of joint angles, and have slightly varying sensor placements and
orientations. Two different types of models include personalized and generalized models. When aiming
to assess the performance of a generalized model, testing should involve recordings from subjects not
included in the training set. Conversely, training and testing datasets should encompass data from the
same subjects for evaluating a personalized model.
Leave-One-Subject-Out (LOSO) validation is a form of cross-validation that involves training the model
on all subjects but one and evaluating it on the remaining subject. This method assesses cross-subject
generalization, uncovering potential biases or limitations specific to individual subjects [62]. If a gen-
eralized model works, user specific training data isn’t needed, and we can use the same model univer-
sally.
14 Tanguy Lewko , 7.3.2024

--- PAGE 22 ---
Master’s Thesis
Figure 3.6: Leave-One-Subject-Out (LOSO) cross-validation process.
In within-subjects validation, each individual contributes to training and testing, capturing subject-
specific patterns in both sets. Approximately 80% of the data from all subjects is utilized for training
and model fitting, with the remaining 20% reserved for independent testing.
Employing both LOSO and within-subjects validation provides a nuanced assessment of the model’s
performance. LOSO enables the evaluation of a generalized model’s performance. At the same time,
within-subject validation offers more comprehensive insights into the model’s performance, accounting
for subject-specific nuances and allowing for rapid prototyping at a smaller computational cost.
3.3.2 Architecture
Given insights from the literature highlighting the effectiveness of LSTM and convolutional layers for
activity recognition, we integrated these into our architecture.
The architecture presented in Figure 3.7 is a hybrid architecture that combines convolutional and
recurrent layers to solve a multi-output classification task, predicting for each timestep both the activity
being performed and which hand is performing. One example of output for a given timestep would be
{brushing teeth, right}, meaning that the network predicts that the subject is brushing his teeth with
his right hand.
The neural network takes an input window of the signal of size ws and with #features as the number
of different input IMU channels. Then, a 1D convolutional layer is used to extract information on
local patterns in the sensor data, followed by a Rectified Liner Unit (ReLU) activation to introduce
non-linearity. Two bidirectional LSTM layers are then used to capture temporal patterns in the data
sequences in the forward and backward directions. Finally, two fully connected layers are used for each
classification task. The network outputs predictions only for the middle part of the signal to avoid
making predictions on a signal that lacks context information.
We implemented multiple regularization techniques such as dropout, which is applied after each biLSTM
layer, and L1 and L2 regularization, with value 10−5
for all model parameters.
15 Tanguy Lewko , 7.3.2024

--- PAGE 23 ---
Master’s Thesis
Figure 3.7: Hybrid architecture: Convolutional and BiLSTM layers
The loss is computed as the sum of the cross-entropy losses of the two classification tasks, and we chose
Adam Optimizer [63] for gradient descent.
For comparison, we share the performance comparison with two other types of neural networks in
Table 3.2, using only forearms IMUs accelerometer and gyroscope signals and within-subject evaluation.
Reported metrics are explained in Appendix A. The LSTM architecture comprises three LSTM layers
with decreasing sizes (256, 128, 64) and produces two sets of predictions with fully connected layers
(output sizes 7 and 3). The biLSTM neural network is similar to the LSTM neural network, except all
three LSTM layers are replaced with bidirectional LSTM layers. Using bidirectional LSTM layers led to
a dramatic improvement in performance in the F1-score of 8.3% for the activity and 6.3% compared to
regular LSTM layers. Replacing the first bi-LSTM layer of the biLSTM network by a 1D convolutional
layer led only to a slight improvement (0.5% in activity and 0.7% in hand) but had the additional
benefit of simplifying the model.

Core(TM) i7-8750H CPU @ 2.20GHz, 2208 MHz, six hearts, 12 logical processors, and an NVIDIA
Quadro P1000 GPU (640 CUDA cores, 4 GB GDDR5 on-board memory, 128-bit memory interface,
82GB/s memory bandwidth).
3.3.3 Feature selection
Feature selection is crucial when developing a deep learning model. Excessive features can lead to data
sparsity, especially in small datasets, potentially resulting in the model overfitting the data. Conversely,
16 Tanguy Lewko , 7.3.2024

--- PAGE 24 ---
Master’s Thesis
too few features might make establishing boundaries between different instances challenging.
As we work with wearable sensors, the practicality and added burden of using more sensors is an
important consideration [29]. The Multi-Sensory dataset comprises five sensors on the upper body: one
on the back, one on each upper arm, and another on each lower arm. The minimum set of sensors
to detect unimanual activities for both arms is one per arm, with the lower arm being intuitively
preferable because of its proximity to the end-effector, i.e., there is greater signal change in a more
distally placed IMU. Additionally, the placement of sensors on the lower arms aligns with the positioning
of smartwatches, which would minimize the system’s invasiveness, practicality, and cost.
Meng et al. (2021) [65] gathered evidence of sensor placement, giving more information. They investi-
gated HAR performance involving stroke survivors using one single sensor from different body positions.
The best accelerometer placements were brachoradialis and extensor carpi ulnaris (both localized on
the forearm).
Table 3.3 compares CNN-biLSTM model performance on different sets of sensors. Interestingly, better
performance was obtained with fewer features, with a 2.7% increase in within-subject F1-Score between
a model with all five sensors and 50 features (x,y,z acceleration and gyroscope data and four quaternions)
and a model taking only data from forearm IMUs and 12 features (acceleration and gyroscope data).
Additionally, we investigated the effect of adding a 50% window overlap, which led to an improvement of
2.2% in the F1-score. It is essential to point out that, contrary to the increase in performance obtained
by selecting fewer features, this performance increase is very costly in terms of computational resources,
effectively doubling the number of windows we train on.
Performance is less good for LOSO cross-validation, with, respectively, 4.3% and 4.2% decrease in
activity and hand F1 score. This can be explained by the fact that the training data does not include
any subject-specific data used for validation. If one subject has a very different way of executing a
motion or sensors are not placed in the same way, it will make it harder to detect by the algorithm that
has not been trained on this kind of data.
Table 3.3: Performance comparison with different sets of features/sensors.
In Figures 3.8 and 3.9, we show the confusion matrices of the best-performing model (CNN-BiLSTM,
forearm IMUs, x, y, z acceleration, and gyroscope data) for within-subject validation. Performance
varies depending on the activity. The best performance is obtained for brushing the teeth (precision =
0.98, recall = 0.98), probably because it is a very salient and specific motion for which the pattern is
more straightforward to distinguish. The worst performance is for the pouring water activity (precision
= 0.79, recall = 0.69), which is much shorter than brushing teeth and more complicated to identify.
17 Tanguy Lewko , 7.3.2024

--- PAGE 25 ---
Master’s Thesis
There is very little confusion between drinking glass and brushing teeth, which both require hand-to-
mouth motions, and we notice that, in general, the inter-class confusion remains very low, most of
the errors involving the negative class. One exception is for pouring water, where 8% of the pouring
water task is confounded with drink glass. We argue that the confusion with the negative class is less
important than between the classes of interest because while they exclude some examples of motion
from the analysis, they do not lead us to analyze some motions wrongly. Finally, the hand confusion
matrix reveals a lower performance for left-hand attributed actions, reflecting that we have a lower
amount of left-handed actions in the dataset: only cleaning the table, pouring water, and drinking from
a glass were done with both right and left arm.

3.3.4 Data augmentations
When faced with a data shortage, data augmentations are an artificial solution to increase the size of
the training set. The primary objective of data augmentation is to enhance the robustness of the trained
model by introducing realistic transformations to the input data that mimic real-world scenarios. Wen et
al. (2021) [66] review time series augmentations for deep learning and propose a taxonomy of time series
augmentation techniques. We focus here on briefly exploring time-domain data augmentations.
Eyobu and Han (2018) applied data augmentations on spectral features data [67]. Um et al.(2017)
[68] investigated data augmentation for wearable sensor data and their protocol to augment the data
increased the classification performance of the motor state of Parkinson’s disease patients from 77.54%
to 86.88%. Uchitomi et al. (2023) also investigated data augmentations to classify Parkinson’s disease
and had the best results with magnitude-domain transformations such as jittering, rotating, and scaling
compared to time-domain transformations such as time warping or cropping [69]. Their experiments
with data augmentations included jittering, scaling, rotating, permuting, magnitude warping, and time
warping. Rotation was identified as having the most significant positive effect on performance.
For time series data augmentation, several commonly utilized methods that we implemented include:
1. Jittering
Jittering aims to increase the robustness of the model to disturbances by adding noise to the data.
When introducing jitter to a signal, it is essential to control the amplitude of the noise to prevent
it from overshadowing the underlying signal. To do so, we define the maximum signal-to-noise
ratio (SNR). The SNR is computed as the ratio of the signal power to the noise power and is
expressed in decibels as follows:
SNRdB = 10log10(Psignal/Pnoise) (3.1)
Where Psignal is the signal power and Pnoise is the noise power, the power is calculated as the
mean value of the squared signal. Once we define a suitable SNR value, we can use it to compute
the maximum noise power:
Pnoise =
Psignal
10(SNRdB/10)
(3.2)
We can then use this noise power to generate a random gaussian noise to add to the signal:
20 Tanguy Lewko , 7.3.2024

--- PAGE 28 ---
Master’s Thesis
Noise ∼ N(0,
p
Pnoise) (3.3)
Jittered signal = Signal + Noise (3.4)
2. Offsetting
The objective of offsetting is to increase the robustness of the model to constant bias by adding or
removing constant value. Similarly to jittering, we compute the maximum offset value by setting
a maximum Signal-to-Offset Ratio (SOR). However, a different random value was added to each
timestep to jitter the signal. To offset the signal, we added the same value to all timesteps.
Poffset =
Psignal
10(SORdB/10)
(3.5)
Offset Value ∼ U

(3.6)
Offsetted Signal = Signal + Offset Value (3.7)
3. Scaling
Scaling is used to make the model robust to variations of sensor sensitivity by multiplying the
signal by a constant value. The effect of scaling is increased on peak values.
Scaled Signal = αs × Signal (3.8)
Where αs is the scaling factor.
4. Zooming
Zooming mimics slowing down all motions by dilating the window in time. We zoom a signal
by selecting a window and dividing the total number of timesteps in the window by a zoom
factor (alphaz), which gives us a reduced number of timesteps. We then select a corresponding
continuous set of timesteps in the signal and scale it back to the original window size using linear
interpolation.
5. Rotating
Rotating simulates minor differences in sensor positioning by rotating the sensors along one of its
axes. Rotation matrices Rx, Ry and Rz for rotating by an angle θ the sensor signal are defined
as:
Rx(θ) =

Master’s Thesis
6. Time warping
Time warping is used to accelerate or slow down some parts of the window to make the model more
robust to different speeds of motion. Our implementation of the time-warping data augmentation
compresses 50% of the data chosen randomly by a compression factor Fc. It dilates the rest of
the data so that the length of the signal stays the same. Compression and dilatation are done
through linear interpolation.
7. Down-sampling
Down-sampling mimics a smaller frequency acquisition rate.
Downsampled Signal = Signal[k · M] (3.12)
where k = 0,1,2,...,

and M is the downsampling factor. ws is the window size.

including jittering, offsetting, scaling, down-sampling, and time warping.

We assign probabilities to each augmentation to control how often it is applied.

More experiments should be conducted in the future to quantify the gain obtained from data aug-

3.4 Conclusion on upper-extremity ADL segmentation
Our activity segmentation pipeline is effective and appropriate for segmenting activities of healthy
participants in active living settings. The boundaries of activities are segmented with great precision
and we achieved an F1-score of 0.87 in within-subjects validation and 0.83 in across-subjects validation.
The 4% decrease in performance when using LOSO validation indicates the importance of incorporating
subject-specific knowledge into the training data. Additionally, our experiments were conducted in a
controlled environment, and it is crucial to explore how this algorithm can generalize to the home
environment. Finally, it is important to investigate how our algorithm would generalize to stroke
patients due to the variability in their motions caused by impairment. To do so, we collect our own
dataset, with a protocol described in Chapter 4. In Chapter 5, we use our algorithm to segment activities
in two mild stroke participants.
This algorithm can be used to quantify the usage of the arms during specific ADLs and enables further
kinematic analysis on pre-segmented ADLs. In Chapter 6, we examine differences in the execution of
specific upper-extremity functional activities of daily living (ADLs) between healthy individuals and
stroke patients.
23 Tanguy Lewko , 7.3.2024

--- PAGE 31 ---
Chapter 4
Collecting an annotated naturalistic
dataset of post-stroke ADLs in a
controlled environment
In this Chapter, we present the protocol used for building a dataset consisting of stroke participants
performing upper-extremity ADLs. This dataset addresses the limitations that open-source datasets
have. It provides synced video data and ground-truth kinematics from optical motion capture.
4.1 Protocol for unstructured ADL data collection
We use the Movella Xsens DOT [70] wearable sensor development platform, which features sensors that
incorporate a 3D accelerometer, gyroscope, and magnetometer. The sensors work wirelessly, making
them suitable for our unstructured ADLs experiment. We use a set of 10 sensors placed on the forehead,
forearms, upper arms, hands, lower back, upper back, and sternum as depicted in Figure 4.1.
Figure 4.1: IMU placement on the upper body
The experiment is recorded using an HD camera that films at 60fps. In addition, Qualysis motion
capture cameras are utilized to capture motion.
24

--- PAGE 32 ---
Master’s Thesis
The signals are acquired and synced using a data acquisition system (Powerlab, ADInstruments) and
recorded with a sampling rate of 200Hz per channel using appropriate software (Labchart, ADInstru-
ments). Participants are screened before the experiment and their fine motor control and mobility levels
are assessed to qualify them for the protocol.
After taking the Fugl-Meyer upper extremity assessment, the participants perform a circuit of ADLs
consisting of washing their face, brushing their teeth, combing hair, applying deodorant, folding a
towel, stirring a pot, pulling a chair to sit, drinking from a bottle, eating with a spoon from a bowl,
and donning a hat. The experimental setup is represented in Figure 4.2, and we illustrate some ADLs
in Figure 4.3. We selected these ADLs because they represent self-feeding and self-grooming tasks,
essential for independence and improvement of quality of life, and reduced caregiver burden.
The circuit is done seven times for each participant under three conditions: A, B, and C. In condition
A, which is repeated three times, participants are asked to perform the task in the same way they would
perform it at home, as naturally as possible. In condition B, performed three times, an occupational
therapist encourages using their impaired (non-dominant for healthy) arm. Finally, in condition C,
participants wear a constraint-induced movement therapy glove (CIMT) (see Figure 4.3) to limit as
much as possible the use of their non-impaired / dominant arm.
Condition A allows us to understand the participants’ natural way of performing ADLs and quantify
the use of their impaired arm across the various activities. It serves as a baseline. Condition B evaluates
the impact of occupational therapist guidance on impaired arm use. Finally, condition C assesses the
feasibility of each activity using only the impaired arm. These conditions allow us to obtain data for
ADLs performed with both arms.
Figure 4.2: 11-ADL circuit set up.
Figure 4.3: Examples of ADLs (CIMT
glove on).
4.2 Labeling methodology
To analyze the data of the unstructured ADL protocol, we label upper extremity ADL segments that
have fixed boundaries, are required to complete activities, and can be potentially valuable for analysis.
A pertinent instance is the motion involved in tooth brushing, which begins with brush contact with
teeth and ends with its disengagement. Reaching motions are omitted from labelization due to their
considerable variability, identification challenges, and lack of clear definition.
25 Tanguy Lewko , 7.3.2024

--- PAGE 33 ---
Master’s Thesis
Each categorized movement is linked to the start and end times, marked by discrete events. The list of
25 labeled ADL segments, together with their respective initiating and concluding events, is presented
in Table 4.1. We also indicate the hand performing the task.
Activity Start Time End Time
Wash face - Hand to face Hand starts moving upward Contact with face

Table 4.1: Definitions of activity labels
We labeled the activities using an open-source Python-based labeling software [71], built with QT, a
cross-platform software for creating applications. Minor modifications were applied to the source code
to suit our application.
The GUI allows one to open a video, visualize it, and move it frame by frame, select frames as the
starting and ending times of an activity, select the activity, and add it. Then, the labels can be
exported as a CSV table. The GUI also supports opening a CSV table to continue previously labeled
videos. Labeling the data from one participant doing the unstructured ADL protocol with the labels
defined in Table 4.1 takes about 3.5 hours and results in approximately fifty segmented actions.

For each ADL run of the dataset, we provide videos (raw and blurred), optical motion capture data files,
video-based labels, and IMU data (raw and synced with labels). On average, every run takes around 3.5
to 7 minutes. However, this duration may vary based on the speed at which the participants complete
the tasks. In each run, there are approximately 50 actions that need to be identified by determining
their start and end frames following the guidelines in Table 4.1.
This dataset was collected close to the end of this thesis, with much time dedicated to data acquisition,
labeling, syncing, and blurring the videos. As a consequence, only a portion of the dataset was prepared
for analysis at the time of the writing. Nonetheless, we were able to construct a proof-of-concept and
some initial testing using the labeled data from stroke participants GG98 and GG102, and healthy
participants UA016, UA020, UA021, and UA025.

Chapter 5
Proof-of-concept on post-stroke
participants
In this Chapter, we present a proof-of-concept of our activity segmentation algorithm on stroke par-
ticipants GG98 and GG102 from our collected data. We use our activity segmentation algorithm to
segment new activities for the participants. We also show that we can decompose segmented activities
even more into analyzable motions using the same algorithm.
5.1 Two-stage activity segmentation
We test our upper extremity activity segmentation algorithm developed in Chapter 3 on our dataset
(see Chapter 4) to verify that our algorithm can effectively be transferred to new tasks performed
by stroke participants. We tested our algorithm on two mildly impaired stroke participants, GG98
(UEFMA=55/60) and GG102 (UEFMA=53/60). The assessment revealed that both GG102 and GG98
lack shoulder abduction and flexion and present diminished coordination and speed. Additionally, GG98
lacks wrist circumduction and GG102 presents some flexor and extensor synergies.
We trained two different models. The first one aims to detect general activities. We selected a subset
of six unimanual tasks (see Table 4.1 for definitions of the tasks): Brush teeth - Brushing, Comb -
Comb, Apply deodorant - Rubbing, Stirring pot - Stirring, Eating (from first Hand-to-Face to last
Recovery), and Drinking (from the start of Hand-To-Face to the end of Recovery). All other motions
are part of the negative class. The second model aims to segment specific motions within a meal, i.e.,
within a combination of eating and drinking events. We segment the transport (lifting the spoon to the
mouth) and recovery (lowering the spoon) phases of eating as well as the transport (lifting the bottle
to the mouth), ingestion (drinking water), and recovery phases of drinking (lowering the bottle from
the mouth to the table). Running the second model results in directly analyzable phases of an activity.
The second model can be applied after the first one outputs the eating and drinking activity segments
as shown in Figure 5.1.
The Multi-Sensory dataset was used to develop our activity segmentation algorithms and had about
15 repetitions of each task for ten subjects. Compared to the Multi-Sensory dataset, our dataset was
much smaller when this thesis was written. We only had access to data from four healthy subjects and
two post-stroke participants. Our dataset consisted of about 2 to 4 samples of the same activity per
hand for each subject. This amount of data is minimal for training a deep-learning algorithm and the
following results should thus be interpreted cautiously.
We conducted two different model training settings. In the first setting, we trained a generalized model
to determine if a model trained on data from four healthy participants could be applied to each stroke
28

--- PAGE 36 ---
Master’s Thesis
Figure 5.1: Two-stage activity segmentation
participant. For this, we used data from UA016, UA020, UA021, and UA025 in the train set, and data
from GG98 and GG102 in the test set.
In the second setting, we trained an individualized model using only data from GG98 and GG102 using
a leave-one-run-out approach. This setting is also known as the individualized setting. Each training
fold was made up of two runs in condition A, two runs in condition B, and one run in condition C. Each
test run consisted of one run in condition A and one run in condition B.
We made no changes to the hyperparameters from the multi-sensory dataset model except for adjusting
the learning rate to achieve a more optimal learning behavior. We could predict our new tasks with
only two examples of each non-negative class in the training set and one for validation. We did not
include data augmentations. Only the forearm accelerations and gyroscope data were used as input.
While the activity segmentation model was trained on complete runs, the meal segmentation model was
only trained on data beginning five seconds before the eating activity and ending five seconds after the
drinking activity.
Table 5.1 presents results for each of the settings for the activity segmentation model. The results were
much better for the individualized models. For subject GG98, we reached F1 scores of 0.87 for the ADL
segmentation and 0.71 for the meal segmentation task. For subject GG102, we obtained F1 scores of
0.88 for the ADL segmentation and 0.82 for the meal segmentation task. These performances come from
very different results across the six runs used in cross-validation, with accuracies as low as 74% and as
high as 96% for ADL segmentation depending on the run. Confusion matrices for the individualized
models are shown in Figures 5.2 and 5.3. We observe that the inter-class confusion is higher for the meal
segmentation algorithm because tasks are shorter and next to each other. For example, lifting the cup
while drinking is confused with tilting the container to drink. For such tasks, it could be interesting to
assess the variation in the ground-truth when multiple people label the same data and compare it to the
segmentation done by the algorithm, as part of the error might come from variations in labels.

Model Accuracy F1-score Accuracy F1-score
GG98 generalized 0.42 0.51 0.22 0.22
GG98 individualized 0.87 0.85 0.71 0.71
GG102 generalized 0.61 0.65 0.67 0.54
GG102 individualized 0.88 0.87 0.84 0.82
Table 5.1: Performance comparison of different models tested on GG98 and GG102.

5.2 Discussion
More data is required both to train and assess the performance of individualized models on stroke
participants but these preliminary results are promising. The challenge will come from obtaining enough
data to capture the variability in ADLs and avoid overfitting. Regarding the generalized models,
the data from the four healthy participants did not generalize at all to the stroke participants. One
reason could be that the post-stroke individuals were performing all motions much slower than the
healthy individuals, or using compensatory strategies. Once more healthy and stroke data is acquired,
generalized models should be tested again on stroke participants. However, healthy data might not
generalize well to the large variance of stroke participants’ patterns used during ADLs, even with more
subjects.
32 Tanguy Lewko , 7.3.2024

--- PAGE 40 ---
Chapter 6
Kinematic disparities between
healthy and post-stroke ADLs with
IMU sensors
In this chapter, we focus on assessing the variations in the performance of particular upper-extremity
functional ADLs, between healthy individuals and stroke patients. Evaluating the quality of motion
post-stroke is necessary for understanding the sensorimotor capabilities of patients. Unlike most existing
literature, which predominantly assesses post-stroke motion by having the stroke survivor perform
structured tasks, we emphasize the importance of evaluating movement quality during unstructured
tasks. Furthermore, our analysis utilizes IMU data, while most existing work relies on optical motion
capture data.
6.1 Task segmentation methodology
To isolate motions of interest within the StrokeRehab dataset [31] activities, we utilized joint angles ob-
tained from the Euler angles computed from the IMU signals. These angles were employed to construct
a simplified 3D geometric model of the human arms, as illustrated in Figure 6.1.
Figure 6.1: Simplified kinematic model of the arms used for visualization.
