Through manual inspection of the IMU signals and derived angles, coupled with an understanding of the
contextual motions, we confidently segmented activities of daily living for further analysis. Specifically,
we focused on the motions associated with brushing teeth and drinking from a container.
6.2 Metrics for motion analysis of ADLs
The most common kinematic deficits for stroke patients during goal-directed motions are longer times to
perform the motions, discontinuous spatial and temporal motion trajectories, and irregular movement
patterns [72, 73, 74]. They also use compensatory movements (e.g., recruiting range of motion from other
joints to compensate for a deficit in another joint) to help with completing tasks. Jayasinghe et al. (2021)
have shown that stroke survivors tend to use more trunk compensation when reaching with their affected
arm compared to their unaffected arm [75]. Wang et al. (2022) conducted a review of technologies
used for compensation assessment and detection during upper extremity (UE) rehabilitation for stroke
patients. The review highlights that wearable IMU sensors can be used for compensation assessment
and detection during structured tasks [76].
Schwarz et al. (2019) give valuable recommendations for kinematic upper limb assessment post-stroke
after reviewing existing work we used for our analysis [77]. Among these recommendations, they suggest
that metrics should be selected based on clinimetric evidence and insights from motor control and that
they should be hypothesis-driven.
We formulate a set of robust metrics to assess potential differences among healthy individuals, those
with mild impairments from stroke, and those with moderate impairments. These metrics aim to
provide a holistic view of the patient’s quality of motion. We divide these metrics into three categories
that cover the different aspects of motion that we identified: range of motion and mobility; temporal
efficiency; and coordination and quality of movement.
Range of motion and mobility
Several studies highlight the importance of Range Of Motion (ROM) in stroke rehabilitation. Stroke
results in a reduced ROM for joints on the paretic side [78]. Beebe and Lang (2019) showed that
measurements of Active Range of Motion (AROM) of the upper extremity taken within one month
after stroke could be used to predict upper extremity function after three months [79]. We investigate
34 Tanguy Lewko , 7.3.2024

--- PAGE 42 ---
Master’s Thesis
mobility-related metrics mainly related to joint angle values. Stroke participants’ motions are highly
variable. Indeed, impairment might vary greatly depending on how the stroke occurred. Different stroke
patients can reach different ROMs, and many tend to use other compensatory motions to overcome their
impairments and still be able to perform the motions. Analyzing the amplitude of joints can reveal
anomalies in use for certain activities.
Temporal efficiency
Temporal efficiency metrics relate to the effectiveness with which participants perform a movement.
One underlying assumption is that because healthy participants do not struggle to do the activities,
they might use less time and generate larger acceleration values. Possible metrics to investigate are
total movement time, time to peak velocity, and velocity and acceleration values.
Coordination and quality of movement
After a stroke, patients tend to present a deficit in inter-joint coordination that can lead to segmented
arm motions. During rehabilitation and recovery, there is evidence that patients regain this smoothness
of motion [80]. To evaluate inter-joint coordination, we focus on smoothness computation and inter-joint
cross-correlation. Cross-correlation measures the correlation between two-time series signals over time.
The result is a correlation coefficient between -1 and 1 that indicates the strength and the direction of
the relationship between the two signals. Smoothness of movement refers to the degree of continuity or
lack of interruption in a motion. It assesses how closely a movement mirrors the pattern of starting with
acceleration and then transitioning into deceleration. Melendez-Calderon et al. (2021) evaluated the
validity of the different smoothness measures derived from IMU measurements [81]. Top approaches
to measuring smoothness include Spectral Arc Length (SPARC) and log dimensionless jerk (LDLJ-
V). It has been concluded that both measures should preferably be used with velocity measurements.
They are prone to errors when applied to translational velocity reconstructed from acceleration due to
drift. In addition, SPARC can be directly applied to rotational velocities, whereas LDLJ-V generates
an error. SPARC [82] has been chiefly used in literature to quantify smoothness in point-to-point
reaching motions in stroke. One of the significant benefits of using this measure is that it computes
in the frequency domain, which means that the length of the motion doesn’t impact the smoothness
calculation. Other metrics, such as trajectory, velocity, and jerk, require adjustments due to changes in
length, but this isn’t the case for SPARC. The main idea behind SPARC computation is that less smooth
movements have more frequency composition when approaching the signal with a Fourier series. Beck
et al. (2018) compared the smoothness of walking using inertial sensors during walking in Parkinson’s
disease, computing SPARC from acceleration and gyroscope data [83]. Garcia et al. (2021) used SPARC
for smoothness analysis of gait using IMUs [84]. Similarly to what they did, we first subtract the mean
of the signal when computing smoothness and apply a cutoff frequency of 10 hertz. SPARC is calculated
on the entire motion. Refai et al. (2021) obtained kinematic and clinical measurements in forty stroke
participants during a reach-to-grasp movement in weeks 1 to 26 post-stroke [85]. The study revealed
that the restoration of smoothness in a reaching task is correlated over time with the recovery from
motor impairment as evaluated by the UEFMA. Until five weeks post-stroke, both SPARC and UEFMA
scoring improved significantly.
The SPARC formula [81] is given by:

With this definition, motions with low SPARC values are unsmooth compared to those with high

6.3 Brushing teeth post-stroke motion analysis
Using the method described in Section 6.1, we were able to extract with high confidence 86 samples
(583 seconds) of healthy subject brushing coming from 18 different subjects, 84 samples (404 seconds)
of mild (FMA 26-52) subject brushing from 19 subjects, and 98 samples (918 seconds) of moderate
(FMA 26-52) subject brushing from 21 subjects.
Motivation for using the toothbrushing ADL for analysis of motor impairment in stroke.
In [86], Inada et al. evaluate the arm joint motion during toothbrushing motion. Their study highlights
that the toothbrushing motion typically falls within the frequency range of 3.9 to 4.5 Hz, that it is
a consistent and synchronous motion across all arm joints, and that the elbow plays a pivotal role in
maintaining stability during brushing. Simkins et al. (2013) [87] investigated the effect of rhythmic
motions on joint synergies between shoulder and elbow rotation after stroke at different speeds. It was
concluded that people with hemiparesis move their arms at a lower frequency when asked to move as
fast as possible. They also use smaller amplitudes, and the more the speed of the rhythmic motion
increases, the more synergies are observed. This motivates the analysis of brushing teeth ADL for
analyzing motor impairment in stroke.
In the following, we showcase, for a selection of selected metrics, the comparisons of their distribution
for healthy, mildly impaired, and moderately impaired subjects. More evaluated metrics can be found
in Table B.3.

teeth, in comparison to healthy individuals. We hypothesize that this increase in angular velocity may
be a compensatory mechanism, which reflects their adaptation to overcome the reduced motor control
caused by the stroke. For instance, if the wrist is unable to move the toothbrush, they rotate their arm
more to compensate for the lack of movement.

Conclusions on stroke vs. healthy participants brushing motion
Our analyses showed that stroke participants use less accelerations, higher rotational velocities, and
smaller shoulder elevation when brushing their teeth. We found no significant difference in elbow joint
angles being used and in the frequency of the brushing motion. The amplitude of the motion is also
larger for healthy individuals compared to post-stroke, as shown by the higher median absolute deviation
of both shoulder flexion, abduction and rotation.
Brushing teeth can contribute to evaluating impairment levels during activities of daily living, as it is a
challenging and constrained activity that requires mobility and coordination in the upper extremities.
While complex ADLs might be more efficient for highlighting differences between healthy and stroke
participants, severely impaired participants would not be able to do them, which is a downside.

--- PAGE 47 ---
Master’s Thesis
6.4 Drinking post-stroke motion analysis
6.4.1 Decomposition of the drinking ADL
The drinking motion during which the hand is in contact with an open container can be decomposed
into three distinct phases based on their kinematic properties, as described by Murphy’s phase distri-
bution:
1. Transport phase: This phase involves elevating the liquid container from the resting position to
the mouth. The primary motions are elbow flexion and shoulder abduction/flexion. As this phase
requires dynamically moving an object, the kinematics can be characterized as dynamic.
2. Ingestion phase: The goal is to stabilize the container while sipping liquid. Minor adjustments
such as forearm rotation or shoulder abduction/flexion may be used to tilt the container precisely.
Compared to the transport phase, this phase emphasizes stability over dynamic movement.
3. Recovery phase: In the recovery phase, the container is lowered back to its original position. This
is accomplished primarily through elbow extension and shoulder flexion/abduction reduction.
Figure 6.9 illustrates this decomposition, indicating key events that mark the start and end of each
phase.
Figure 6.9: Decomposition of the drinking task.
By analyzing each drinking phase separately based on their distinct kinematic properties, we can de-
velop a more scientifically rigorous understanding of the biomechanics underlying this everyday task.
The drinking ADL has been well studied, mainly in structured experiments isolating each phase and
with motion capture systems. It has been much less studied using wearable sensors in unstructured
settings.
In [88], Murphy et al. evaluated the change of a set of kinematical parameters describing movement time,
velocity, strategy, interjoint coordination, and compensatory movement between stroke and healthy par-
ticipants during drinking task using motion capture. They found that the number of movement units,
total movement time, and peak angular velocity of the elbow were the best features to discriminate be-
tween healthy, mild, and moderate groups, with the number of movement units being the best indicator
of motion quality. They also showed that time is correlated with number of movement units.
Kim et al. (2014) [89] conducted a study identifying kinematic differences between 16 hemiplegic
and 32 healthy participants during drinking phases. The hemiplegic group took longer to achieve the
drinking task, taking extra care when lifting the cup to avoid spilling water and caring less during
recovery. Interestingly, hemiplegic participants used more extensive abduction in all phases of drinking
and smaller flexion in the shoulder joint for the transporting and ingestion phases.
40 Tanguy Lewko , 7.3.2024

--- PAGE 48 ---
Master’s Thesis
6.4.2 Analysis
We analyze both dynamic phases of the drinking task with the same set of metrics. Using the segmenta-
tion method described in Section 6.1, we could confidently isolate the transport, ingestion, and recovery
phases of drinking. For each stage, we could isolate 70 samples from 15 mildly impaired participants, 78
samples from 18 moderately impaired participants, and 86 samples from 18 healthy subjects, totaling
234 drinking samples analyzed. As for the toothbrushing ADL, we only discuss here a subset of the
analyzed metrics, more detailed analysis can be found in Tables B.1 and B.2.

6.5 Conclusion on post-stroke upper-extremity motion analy-
sis within ADLs
In conclusion, our study on the drinking and tooth-brushing motions gives us important insights into
how people who have had a stroke compare to those who have not. Although specific measurements
help to separate the two groups, there is still some overlap between the distributions of the different
groups.
The metrics investigated (see Tables B.3, B.1 and B.2) include some descriptive statistics such as
medians, 95th percentile, and median absolute deviation calculated on the forearm and upper arm
42 Tanguy Lewko , 7.3.2024

--- PAGE 50 ---
Master’s Thesis
norms of acceleration and angular velocity. These descriptive statistics are robust versions of mean,
peak, and standard deviation. For the toothbrushing ADL, we also looked at shoulder abduction,
rotation, and flexion as most of the motion comes from the shoulder. Then, for drinking tasks, we
added total movement time and SPARC to measure smoothness and cross-correlation between forearm
and upper arm angular velocities and accelerations. These additional task-specific metrics have been
shown to effectively distinguish between the movements of participants who have had a stroke and
healthy participants. Comparison between healthy, mildly impaired, and moderately impaired subjects
can be found in Appendix B.
Our findings suggest stroke survivors are likelier to present heavy tails in bio-mechanical metrics that
translate a motion’s quality aspect. Looking at specific aspects like SPARC and movement time, we
notice interesting differences between stroke and healthy participants. While some stroke survivors
move similarly to healthy individuals, many show less smooth motions and take more time to finish
tasks. This highlights the fact that the experiences of stroke survivors can vary widely.
It is crucial to recognize the limitations of our study, like the limited range of motions and instances
we analyzed. Future research with a broader set of motions and a larger dataset will help us better
understand the subtleties of how motor skills play out in stroke survivors during activities of daily
living.
43 Tanguy Lewko , 7.3.2024

--- PAGE 51 ---
Chapter 7
The motion healthiness score: A
data-driven framework for
naturalistic motion quality
assessment
While UE motor impairment assessments like the UEFMA or the ARAT provide valuable informa-
tion about upper extremity motor function, that can help treatment planning and track rehabilitation
progress, they do not capture patients’ capacity to perform specific functional tasks. For example, Mur-
phy et al.[90] showed that kinematic movement performance measures obtained during a drinking task,
such as movement time, smoothness, and angular velocities, correlate much more with activity capacity
than with actual impairment level obtained through UEFMA and ARAT. Assessing impairment in a
functional setting holds considerable promise to understand activity capacity better.
In an attempt to replicate the FMA score from wearable sensors, Yu et al. (2016) employed two
accelerometers and seven flex sensors to monitor the function of the upper limb [91]. The proposed
quantitative FMA model based on wearable sensor data can precisely predict the FMA scores, with a
coefficient of determination of up to 0.917. Chaeibakhsh et al. (2016) used accelerometer and gyroscope
data to score UEFMA using machine learning algorithms [92]. Although these works offer a good
opportunity to do assessments at home, without the need for a therapist, impairment is still evaluated
on very structured tasks. Oubre et al. (2020) [93] proposed an approach to estimate upper-limb
impairment in stroke survivors by using two wearable inertial sensors on the wrist and sternum and
evaluating on two minutes of continuous random voluntary upper limb movements spanning the entire
range of motion. They achieved a root mean square error of 18.2% for 23 stroke survivors. Vanmechelen
et al. (2023) conducted a scoping review on using wearable sensors to assess movement disorders during
upper limb tasks. The review found that most of the assessments were carried out during structured
tasks and identified commonly computed metrics that are used to identify different kinds of impairments
[94].
In Chapter 6, we observed distinct distributions between the Healthy, Mild, and Moderate participant
groups for the identified set of robust wearable-IMU-based metrics. This suggests that valuable informa-
tion about motion quality is contained within the IMU data during specific constrained ADL segments.
Within this chapter, our primary objective is to develop a method to incorporate identified metrics into
a framework for the assessment of naturalistic motion quality. We aim to calculate a Motion Healthiness
Score (MHS) for each movement by integrating various metrics related to mobility, time efficiency, and
overall motion characteristics.
44

--- PAGE 52 ---
Master’s Thesis
The fundamental concept behind the MHS we develop is to gauge the disparity between the motion
under evaluation and the same motion executed by healthy subjects. This approach is based on the
assumption that the standard for high-quality of motion is established by the movements of healthy
individuals. We take into account the substantial variability in stroke impairments among individuals:
some stroke participants may execute certain motions with proficiency while struggling with others.
Furthermore, a fundamental principle of stroke rehabilitation is to gradually align movements with
those that healthy individuals would typically perform, and this score measures the quality of the
alignment. The proposed score has convenient applications. It could be communicated to therapists
and patients to monitor rehabilitation and gauge progress in motion performance. Therapists could use
this information to emphasize training for motions with lower MHS to optimize recovery.
7.1 Methods and results
In this Section, we explain the derivation of the MHS and compute the MHS for StrokeRehab partici-
pants in three motions: brushing teeth, the transport phase of drinking (lifting the container), and the
recovery phase of drinking (lowering the container).
Figure 7.1 shows the principal steps of the MHS framework. The first step is to pre-segment a motion of
interest, this can be done either manually or using our activity segmentation algorithm (see Chapter 3).
Then, we compute a set of robust metrics, as defined in Chapter 6. Subsequent steps involve reducing
the dimensionality of the metrics using PCA and computing the distance between each motion and
healthy references for that motion in the principal component space. More detailed explanations of
these steps will follow in the following sections.
Figure 7.1: Motion healthiness score (MHS) framework
7.1.1 PCA dimensionality reduction
In Chapter 6, we identified a set of robust descriptive statistics and task-specific metrics, that are
interpretable, and allow for Healthy, Mild, and Moderate group differentiation. We first compute these
metrics for each pre-segmented motion.
Subsequently, employing Principal Component Analysis (PCA), we reduce the dimensionality of the
computed metrics, optimizing the retained variance. A desirable property of PCA is its orthogonality:
principal components are orthogonal to each other, which makes them linearly independent. Each
principal component captures a non-redundant aspect of the data.
To apply PCA, we first compute the covariance matrix Σ:
45 Tanguy Lewko , 7.3.2024

--- PAGE 53 ---
Master’s Thesis
Σ =
1
n − 1
(X − X̄)T
(X − X̄) (7.1)
with X the data matrix, X̄ the mean of each feature and n the number of features.
We then compute the eigenvalues λi of the covariance matrix by solving the following:
det(Σ − λI) = 0 (7.2)
and solve for the eigenvectors vi by substituting each eigenvalue into:
(Σ − λiI)vi = 0 (7.3)
We then sort the eigenvalues in descending order and select all λi > 1 following the Guttman-Kaiser
criterion [95]. This criterion is based on the argument that no component explaining less than the
variance of an original variate represents a significant source dimension. Although it may not be
optimal in all situations, it is a widely-spread, easy-to-use method for selecting the number of principal
components. We select the corresponding eigenvectors to form the projection matrix W.
W = [v1,v2,...,vk]
Where k is the number of eigenvalues greater than 1.
Finally, we can project the data matrix X in the subspace of principal components defined by the
eigenvectors:
Y = XW (7.4)
Figure 7.2 shows the scree plots for the three tasks we analyze. The Guttman-Kaiser criterion keeps the
six first principal components for the brushing teeth activity, five for the drinking transport activity,
and five for the drinking recovery activity, leading to respectively 88%, 84%, and 86% of explained
variance retained.
(a) Brushing teeth (b) Drinking transport (c) Drinking recovery
Figure 7.2: Scree plots for brushing teeth, drinking transport and recovery PCA

Master’s Thesis
7.1.2 Mahalanobis distance to healthy data
The Mahalanobis distance [96] measures the distance between a point and a distribution under the
assumption that the data conforms to a multivariate normal distribution. This distance metric is
more relevant than the Euclidean distance because it incorporates the covariance structure of the data,
allowing for considering correlations between variables. It is computed as:
D2
M = (x − m)T
· C−1
· (x − m) (7.5)
Where D2
M is the square of the Mahalanobis distance, x is the observation vector, m is the mean of
each variable, and C is the covariance matrix of the variables.
We use the Mahalanobis-MCD distance, which is known as a robust criterion for outlier detection.
Instead of computing the mean and covariance matrix of the whole data, it uses the minimum covariance
determinant (MCD) method to estimate the multivariate mean and covariance matrix using a subset
of the data so that we minimize the influence of anomalies on their computations. Following the
recommendations in [97], we use a support fraction of 0.75 when calculating the MCD. We use the
Mahalanobis-MCD distance to compute the distance from sample motions to the distribution of healthy
in the principal components subspace. For the sake of simplicity, we will refer to the Mahalanobis-MCD
distance as Mahalanobis distance going forward.
The square of the Mahalanobis distance can be approximated by a Chi-square distribution, with a
degree of freedom equal to the number of principal components. We use the quantile value 0.95 as a
threshold to define the limit of what is considered healthy data. Any point with a Mahalanobis distance
superior to the threshold value set using the Chi-Square distribution is regarded as an outlier. Any
point within the threshold is given a maximum MHS, meaning the motion is considered healthy. To
give an intuition on the method, we show in Figures 7.3, 7.4 and 7.5 the projection of metrics in the
3D space defined by the three first principal components, with, in green the ellipsoid of healthy data
defined with this threshold. We observe that most of the healthy data fall into this ellipsoid, while mild
and moderate samples are more dispersed. A black dot marks points outside of the ellipsoid. We refer
to these points as outliers.
Figure 7.3: Brushing teeth PCA projection (3D)

Although we do not have a ground truth for how far a motion is to healthy data, we verify that our
distance behaves well by demonstrating that mild group samples have a smaller distance to healthy
data than moderate, by computing the correlation between the UE-FMA score and the distance for
each sample, as well as by evaluating the variation of the resulting score from different samples of the
same subject. We also evaluate the correlation between the scores obtained for each of the three tasks
we examine.
We provide the Bhattacharyya distance [98] to measure overlap and convergence between distribu-

We examined the Pearson correlation between brushing teeth, drinking transport, and drinking recovery
distances to healthy data. The correlation coefficient between brushing and drinking transport Maha-
lanobis distances to the healthy ellipsoid is 0.59, indicating a moderate positive correlation. Brushing
and recovery distances are correlated at 0.62, while transport and recovery distances show a notably
strong correlation at 0.91. All distances are moderately or strongly correlated, with a very high corre-
lation for each individual between the transport and recovery phases of drinking.
From the Mahalanobis distances computation, we define the MHS as follows. The best attainable MHS
for a task is 10, obtained when the Mahalanobis distance to the healthy distribution is less than the
distance defined by the 0.95 quantile of the chi-square distribution with a degree of freedom equal to
the number of selected principal components. The worst score is 0 when the Mahalanobis distance to
the healthy cluster is superior to the 0.95 quantile distance estimated with a Kernel Density Estimation
(KDE) of stroke participants’ distances. These two distance thresholds are shown in Figures 7.6, 7.7
and 7.8. Between these two values, the score is linearly interpolated using the piecewise linear function
described in Equation 7.7:
MHS = 10 − (DB − th) ×
10
ts − th
(7.7)
With th the 0.95 quantile of the chi-square distribution with a degree of freedom equal to the number
of selected principal components, and ts the 0.95 quantile distance estimated with a Kernel Density
Estimation (KDE) of stroke participants’ distances.
We use Silverman’s bandwidth estimation for the KDE [99].
The mean Mahalanobis distance to the healthy distribution and the resulting MHS for each subject and
each activity are reported in Table 7.2 and shown in Figures 7.9, 7.10 and 7.11.

We computed the standard deviation in MHS ratings of the different samples of a subject performing
the same activity. The mean standard deviation was 0.56 for brushing teeth, 0.60 for drinking transport,
and 0.70 for drinking recovery. This highlights consistency in the score as the rating does not vary a
lot between motions performed by the same subject.
We also quantified the separability power of the MHS by optimizing a threshold to maximize the
accuracy to predict if the person doing the motion is healthy or has had a stroke. Each motion rated
above the threshold is classified as healthy and below as belonging to an impaired participant. The
optimal thresholds for brushing teeth, drinking transport, and drinking recovery scores were respectively
9.9, 9.3, and 9.5, leading to accuracies of 0.76, 0.82, and 0.84.

threshold are respectively 9.9, 9.3 and 9.5 for brushing teeth, drinking transport, and drinking recovery.
We analyzed the correlation between UEFMA score and brushing teeth, drinking transport, and drinking
recovery MHS. The correlation coefficients were 0.37, 0.43, and 0.47, respectively.
7.2 Discussion
We have developed a new data-driven framework called the motion healthiness score (MHS) to evaluate
the quality of naturalistic motion. The MHS framework incorporates various metrics to assess the
distance between a motion being evaluated and the same motion performed by healthy individuals.
The framework has shown good properties like high consistency when rating sample motions from the
same subject and good separability with over 80% accuracy between healthy and post-stroke individuals.
It provides an opportunity to evaluate a person’s impairment in a functional setting without the need
for a therapist’s evaluation.
This framework offers multiple advantages and can be used to analyze a wide range of motions in both
structured and unstructured tasks. A normative dataset is utilized to define what constitutes a healthy
motion, without relying on the UEFMA, which does not correlate well with activity capacity. The MHS
is an interpretable measure of motion quality and could be used to identify motions that require further
training at home. Compared to other impairment measures like UEFMA, the MHS allows for more
sensitivity in the moderate and severe range, as there is no maximum distance to healthy data. The
MHS provides an opportunity to move impairment measurements into the functional place and could
therefore correlate better than other assessments with arm use and independence.
We have identified some areas that require further consideration before using the MHS measure. This
measure needs additional validation and future studies should investigate the effect of varying the
selected metrics. Although the rating system has desirable properties, its correlation with expert-
perceived motion quality should be investigated. Additionally, the scoring system assumes that a stroke
participant’s motion should approximate that of a healthy participant during recovery. However, the
optimal motion solution for a participant with a stroke may differ significantly from that of a healthy
participant. One key question to answer is defining the Minimal Clinically Important Difference (MCID)
of the distance to healthy data. Using the MHS to track the four to twelve weeks of recovery that take
place during outpatient therapy could offer a better understanding of this impairment measure.
One limitation is that the data needs to conform to a multivariate normal distribution. For some
activities, there could be different clusters of how healthy people perform an activity. For example,
brushing hair and combing hair might produce different measurements of a similar task. In such cases,
it may be considered to create more than one ellipsoid for the healthy data, with two or more regions of
the PC space being associated with healthy behavior. Including information on the age and gender of
the subject can also be beneficial as motions can vary significantly with age, resulting in slower motions,
for example.

Chapter 8
Conclusion
In conclusion, this research aimed to investigate the ability of inertial measurement units (IMUs) to
segment and analyze upper extremity (UE) movements during activities of daily living (ADLs). The
capability to do so could help encourage stroke survivors to use their affected arm more throughout the
day. We have demonstrated the ability to accurately segment UE ADLs from raw IMU data using a deep
learning algorithm that utilizes both CNN and biLSTM layers. While most existing work focuses on
classifying a pre-segmented window as part of an activity, we focused on precisely segmenting continuous
non-pre-segmented data. The algorithm was tested on ten healthy participants from the Multi-Sensory
dataset. The six segmented activities were opening and closing a door, brushing teeth, drinking from
a glass, pouring water, and cleaning a table. One of the unique features of our algorithm is the use of
context-aware predictions, taking into account past and future data. We achieved respectively F1-scores
of 0.83 in across-subject validation and 0.87 in within-subject validation, using only two IMUs located
on the forearms. We proposed a methodology for collecting an annotated naturalistic IMU-based ADL
dataset in a controlled environment, using video ground truth to reliably label ADLs. We collected data
from five stroke patients and five healthy participants and used this data to demonstrate the proof-
of-concept of our UE ADL segmentation algorithm on two stroke patients. Our results highlight the
potential need for tailored models for post-stroke individuals due to their high motion variability. From
the StrokeRehab open-source dataset, we isolated a total of 182 samples of stroke participants brushing
their teeth and 148 sample drinking events. In addition, we gathered 86 samples of healthy participants
brushing their teeth and 88 samples of healthy participants drinking. Based on the wearable sensor
data, we identified robust metrics that can be directly computed and effectively distinguish between
healthy and stroke participants’ motions during these two ADLs. Finally, we developed a method
to aggregate these metrics into a Motion Healthiness Score (MHS). This score uses the Mahalanobis
distance to measure the disparity between the movement of a stroke survivor and the same motion
executed by healthy subjects. It showed good properties such as high consistency when rating sample
motions from the same subject and good separability (>80% accuracy) between healthy and post-stroke
individuals.
We want to acknowledge certain limitations of our study despite the promising results. (1) The first
limitation of this research comes from the use of open-source datasets with important information
missing. The datasets we used did not include video data, which made it difficult to interpret the
results of our algorithms. For example, we were unable to determine why the algorithm made certain
false detections for activity segmentation. Additionally, for the motion healthiness score, we could not
verify whether motions that were considered close to healthy appeared healthy or not. The StrokeRehab
dataset also lacked crucial information, such as the age of healthy subjects. (2) Activity segmentation
should still be evaluated in stroke participants with moderate or severely affected stroke participants. (3)
Our algorithms were tested in controlled environments and we need to evaluate their performance in a
home setting. (4) Our analysis of motion quality left out some important aspects such as compensation,
which is a good indicator of bad use. (5) The MHS requires further evaluation. Analysis should be
54

--- PAGE 62 ---
Master’s Thesis
extended for more tasks, and the minimal clinically important differences (MCID) remain to determine
for different tasks.
We also highlight some future steps that should be taken to further advance toward a home-based system
for monitoring rehabilitation progress at home. (1) An effort should be made to reduce the cost of data
collection or the quantity of data required by deep learning algorithms. Indeed, data collection and
labeling through video is a very expensive process. One solution could be the self-labeling of data by the
user who records his motion by pressing a button on an app. We can also investigate methods such as
self-supervised learning to reduce the reliance on labeled data. (2) We believe it is important to collect
data at home to test the performance of the algorithms in an uncontrolled setting. (3) The algorithm
for activity segmentation should also be adapted for bi-manual tasks, as stroke participants tend to
use both their arms even for typically considered uni-manual tasks like brushing teeth when trying to
integrate their affected arm into tasks, as they might lack the ability to use only the impaired arm. More
testing on impaired participants is required. (4) Further evaluating the optimal number of wearable
IMU sensors to not burden the user and still be able to provide useful information is required. Different
configurations can go from only one IMU on the paretic forearm, to multiple sensors, potentially able
to provide more information on joint angles and compensation strategies. Acceptability by the end user
is critical and this is an important trade-off. (5) The MHS could be validated either by having multiple
OTs rating motions and checking the correlation with the MHS, or by following patients’ recovery
post-stroke.

Appendix A
Evaluation metrics for activity
segmentation
Confusion matrix
The confusion matrix is a pivotal tool for assessing the performance of classification models. Represented
as a table, the confusion matrix compares the actual classifications of instances with the predictions
made by the model. Let C be the confusion matrix, where Cij denotes the count of instances belonging
to class i that were predicted as class j. The matrix is organized into rows and columns, where each
row corresponds to the instances in a true class, and each column represents the instances predicted
by the model for a given class. The diagonal elements (Cii) signify the number of correct predictions
for each class, while the nondiagonal elements indicate misclassifications. The confusion matrix can be
expressed as follows.
C =





C11 C12 ··· C1n
C21 C22 ··· C2n
. . .
. . .
...
. . .
Cn1 Cn2 ··· Cnn





This detailed breakdown allows for a nuanced understanding of a model’s performance, enabling the
computation of various metrics such as accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 score, which are crucial for a
comprehensive evaluation of the model’s effectiveness in handling multiple classes.
Accuracy
The accuracy of a classifier with multiple labels is computed as follows:
Accuracy =
Pn

Pn

Pn
j=1 Cij
(A.1)
Where:
• Accuracy is the ratio of correctly predicted instances to the total number of instances.
• C is the confusion matrix, where Cij represents the number of instances of class i that were
predicted as class j.
• n is the number of classes in the classification problem.

Multi-Class F1 Score
The F1 score is a widely used metric for assessing the performance of a classifier, particularly in scenarios
with imbalanced class distribution. In the context of a multi-class classification task, the F1 score for
each class can be expressed in terms of the confusion matrix:
Precision(class = a) =
Caa
Pn
i=1 Cia
(A.2)
Recall(class = a) =
Caa
Pn
i=1 Cai
(A.3)
F1 Score(class = a) =
2 × Precision(class = a) × Recall(class = a)
Precision(class = a) + Recall(class = a)
(A.4)
The F1 scores for each class can then be averaged in different ways. Standard averaging methods include
the weighted average, which uses the number of samples as weights; the macro average, the arithmetic
mean of the F1 scores; and the micro average, equal to the overall accuracy.
For a multiclass classification task, let F1(class = a) represent the F1 score for class a as computed in
Equation (3). Then, the averaging methods are defined as follows:
1. Weighted Average:
Weighted F1 =
Pn

Comprehensive metrics for continuous activity recognition
In [100], the authors insist that standard evaluation metrics borrowed from the pattern recognition
field fail to capture common artifacts in continuous activity recognition, such as event fragmentation,
event merging, or timing offsets. Their goal was to characterize performance by showing the algorithm’s
strengths and weaknesses.
They report true positives and true negatives as well as the following types of error [58]:
• Overfill and underfill. Overfill occurs when a start label starts before the actual start time of the
activity or when a stop ends after the end of the class. Conversely, underfill happens when the
start is after the actual activity starts or the stop is before.
• Insertion: Predicting an activity when the ground truth is negative class.
• Fragmentation: Error of predicting the negative class between an uninterrupted activity class.
• Deletion: Assigning a negative class label where there is an activity.
• Substitution: Activity is classified as a different class than the negative one.
